title: The First Document Request: What It Reveals About Your Business Before Price Ever Comes Up
linkedin:
Most business owners assume the hardest part of selling is agreeing on price.

It usually isn't. The harder moment comes earlier, the day a buyer or their accountant sends through a routine document request: three years of financials, a customer list, key contracts, the lease, a staff structure.

Nothing about that list is unusual. Almost every business has these documents somewhere. What it actually tests is whether the business can produce a clean, consistent version of itself on demand, without weeks of digging and without the numbers contradicting what the owner remembers.

Two businesses can hand over identical figures and be read completely differently, purely on how quickly and calmly the file comes together. A business that answers within a week or two signals it already knows itself. One that takes six weeks and three versions of the same spreadsheet signals risk, whatever the underlying numbers actually show.

Buyers price uncertainty as much as they price profit. That pricing starts long before a formal valuation conversation does.

The businesses that handle this well didn't get lucky with tidy books. They built the file before there was a buyer to send it to.

A note for business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria who are even loosely thinking about a future sale, or just want a tidier business.

Long before a buyer talks price, they send a routine document request: financial statements, a customer list, key contracts, the lease, a staff structure. It looks procedural, but it is actually the first real test a buyer runs. Not on whether the numbers are good, but on whether the business can produce a clean, consistent version of itself without weeks of digging.

Two businesses can hand over identical figures and be read completely differently, purely on how quickly and calmly that file comes together. A fast, tidy answer signals a business that already knows itself. A slow, scrambled one signals risk, and that risk gets priced in long before any formal number is discussed.

The businesses that handle this well built the file before there was ever a buyer to send it to, which also happens to make the business easier to run day to day.

Read the full piece on the blog for the handful of gaps that trip up even well-run businesses, and how to close them early.
